title: Remark
body_md: It will follow from \cite[Corollary~1]{KNT} that no hypersurfaces of constant sectional curvature exist in the product of \emph{more than two} space forms (no more than one of which being flat). Thus, the results presented in this paper complete the classification of hypersurfaces of constant sectional curvature in arbitrary products of space forms.

label: splits
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{splits}
     For a hypersurface $f\colon M^{n}\to \overline{M}^{k}(\kappa_1)\times \overline{M}^{n-k+1}(\kappa_2)$, $2\leq k\leq n-1$, the following are equivalent:
     \begin{enumerate}[label={{\rm(\alph*)}}]
         \item $f$ is locally decomposable.
         \item The tangent vector field $\zeta$ vanishes everywhere.
         \item The product angle function $C\equiv \pm 1$.
         \item $\dim\ker \mathcal{R} = k$ or $\dim\ker (I-\mathcal{R})=n-k+1$ everywhere.
     \end{enumerate}
     Moreover, if, in addition, $M^n$ is complete and simply connected, then any of the above conditions implies that $f$ is decomposable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The equivalence between (a) and (b) is a particular case of \cite[Proposition~3.3]{MeT1}. By the third equation in \eqref{propR},  $\zeta$ vanishes everywhere if and only if $t=0$ or $t=1$ everywhere. By \eqref{angle}, this holds if and only if $C=1$ or $C=-1$ everywhere, respectively. Thus, (b) and (c) are equivalent. Finally, by the discussion after \eqref{propR}, $\zeta$ vanishes everywhere if and only if $\dim \ker \mathcal{R} + \dim \ker (I-\mathcal{R})=n$ everywhere. The equivalence between (b) and (d) then follows from \eqref{dimkerR}.  The last assertion is also a consequence of \cite[Proposition~3.3]{MeT1}.

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to show that the one-form $\zeta^\flat =\<\zeta,\cdot\>$ is closed. Since $S\mathcal{R} = \mathcal{R} S$, the endomorphism $A:=(tI-\mathcal{R})S$ is symmetric. Then, using~\eqref{derS2}, a direct computation yields
    $d\zeta^\flat (X,Y) = \<AX,Y\> - \<AY,X\> = 0$ for all $X,Y\in\Gamma(TM^n)$. Thus, $d\zeta^\flat = 0$.

label: lem:rks01
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:rks01}
    Let $f\colon M^{n}\to \overline{M}^{k}(\kappa_1)\times \overline{M}^{n-k+1}(\kappa_2)$, $2\leq k\leq n-1$, $\kappa_1\kappa_2\neq 0$, be a hypersurface. If $M^n$ has constant sectional curvature, then $\operatorname{rk} S\ge2$ everywhere on $M^n$.
head: environment

label: Gaussrankone
title: Proof
body_md:
Arguing by contradiction, suppose that $\operatorname{rk} S \le 1$ at some $x\in M^n$. Then the Gauss equation \eqref{Gauss} gives
    \begin{equation}\label{Gaussrankone}
    R(X,Y) = \kappa_1(X\wedge Y - X\wedge\mathcal{R} Y - \mathcal{R} X \wedge Y) + (\kappa_1+\kappa_2)(\mathcal{R} X \wedge \mathcal{R} Y)
    \end{equation}
    for all $X,Y\in T_xM^n$.  Since $2\leq k\leq n-1$, by \eqref{dimkerR} we can choose nonzero
$X_1\in \ker \mathcal{R}$ and $X_2\in \ker(I-\mathcal{R})$, and \eqref{Gaussrankone} gives $R(X_1, X_2)=0$. 
If $\zeta\neq 0$ at $x$, applying \eqref{Gaussrankone}  to $X_i$ and $\zeta$,  $i=1,2$, yields
$0=R(X_1, \zeta)=\kappa_1(1-r)(X_1\wedge \zeta)$ and $0=R(X_2, \zeta)=\kappa_2r (X_2\wedge \zeta)$, a contradiction.
If $\zeta=0$ at $x$, then either $\ker \mathcal{R}$ or   $\ker (I-\mathcal{R})$, say, the former, has dimension at least two. Applying \eqref{Gaussrankone} to linearly independent $X_1, Y_ 1\in \ker \mathcal{R}$ yields $0=R(X_1, Y_1)=\kappa_1 (X_1\wedge Y_1)$, again a contradiction.  The statement follows.

label: ex:int1
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:int1}
    Let $2\le k \le n-1$ and let $\tilde{\pi}_1\colon\mathbb{R}^{n+3,1}\to \mathbb{R}^{k+1}$ and $\tilde{\pi}_2\colon \mathbb{R}^{n+3,1}\to\mathbb{R}^{n-k+2,1}$ be orthogonal projections. Define
    \[
    \overline{M}^{k,0}(\kappa_1) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{k+1} \, | \, \<x,x\> = \kappa_1^{-1}\},\,\,\, \overline{M}^{n-k+1,0}(\kappa_2) = \{y \in \mathbb{R}^{n-k+2,1} \, | \, \<y,y\> = \kappa_2^{-1}\}
    \]
 and 
 $$\overline{M}^{n+2,1}(\kappa) = \{z \in \mathbb{R}^{n+3,1} \, | \, \<z,z\> = \kappa^{-1}\},$$
  where $\kappa^{-1}=\kappa_1^{-1}+\kappa_2^{-1}$, and where we have $\kappa_2 < 0 < \kappa_1$ and $\kappa_1+\kappa_2 <0$ (and so $\kappa > 0$). 
  Clearly $\overline{M}^{k,0}(\kappa_1) \times \overline{M}^{n-k+1,0}(\kappa_2) \subset \overline{M}^{n+2,1}(\kappa) $.

  Let $w \in \mathbb{R}^{n+3,1}$ be a light-like vector. Denote $w_i = \tilde{\pi}_i(w)$,  for $i=1,2$. We can assume that $\<w_1 ,w_1\> = 1$ and $\<w_2 ,w_2\> = -1$. Let $\mathbb{R}^{n+1} = \operatorname{Span}(w_1 , w_2)^\perp$ and let $\iota\colon \overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa) \to \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ be the isometric embedding of the sphere $\overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)$ such that $\<\iota(p), \iota(p)\>=\kappa^{-1}$. Define the embedding $\phi\colon\overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa) \to \mathbb{R}^{n+3,1}$ by $\phi(p) = \iota(p) + \upsilon(p) w$ for $p \in \overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)$, where we specify the function $\upsilon\colon \overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa) \to \mathbb{R}$ a little later. Note that $w\in \operatorname{Span}(w,\iota(p))^\perp$, for all $p \in \overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)$, by construction.

  We have $\<\phi(p),\phi(p)\> = \<\iota(p),\iota(p)\> = \kappa^{-1}$, and so $\phi(\overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)) \subset \overline{M}^{n+2,1}(\kappa)$. Moreover, since $w$ is light-like and is orthogonal to $\iota(p)$, the embedding $\phi$ is an isometry. To ensure that $\phi(\overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)) \subset \overline{M}^{k,0}(\kappa_1)\times\overline{M}^{n-k+1,0}(\kappa_2)$, we choose the function $\upsilon\colon\overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa) \to \mathbb{R}$ in the definition of $\phi$ in such a way that $\<\tilde{\pi}_1 (\phi(p)),\tilde{\pi}_1 (\phi(p))\>= \kappa_1^{-1}$. 
  This gives $\upsilon(p)= (\kappa_1^{-1}-\<\tilde{\pi}_1 (\iota(p)),\tilde{\pi}_1 (\iota(p))\>)^{1/2}$. Hence
  $$\<\tilde{\pi}_1 (\iota(p)),\tilde{\pi}_1 (\iota(p))\><\<\iota(p),\iota(p)\> = \kappa^{-1}= \kappa_1^{-1}+\kappa_2^{-1} < \kappa_1^{-1},$$ so the right-hand side is well defined. Note that $$\phi(\overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)) =(\overline{M}^{k,0}(\kappa_1) \times \overline{M}^{n-k+1,0}(\kappa_2))\cap w^\perp \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+3,1}.$$

label: ex:int2
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:int2}
     Let $2\le k \le n-1$ and let $\tilde{\pi}_1\colon\mathbb{R}^{n+3,2}\to \mathbb{R}^{k+1,1}$ and $\tilde{\pi}_2\colon \mathbb{R}^{n+3,2}\to\mathbb{R}^{n-k+2,1}$ be orthogonal projections. For $\kappa_1,\kappa_2<0$, define
    \[
    \overline{M}^{k,0}(\kappa_1) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{k+1,1} \, | \, \<x,x\> = \kappa_1^{-1}\},\,\,\, \overline{M}^{n-k+1,0}(\kappa_2) = \{y \in \mathbb{R}^{n-k+2,1} \, | \, \<y,y\> = \kappa_2^{-1}\}
    \]
 and 
 $$\overline{M}^{n+2,1}(\kappa) = \{z \in \mathbb{R}^{n+3,2} \, | \, \<z,z\> = \kappa^{-1}\},$$
  where $\kappa^{-1}=\kappa_1^{-1}+\kappa_2^{-1}$. 
  Clearly $\overline{M}^{k,0}(\kappa_1) \times \overline{M}^{n-k+1,0}(\kappa_2) \subset \overline{M}^{n+2,1}(\kappa) $.

  Let $w\in\mathbb{R}^{n+3,2}$ be such that $\<w,w\>=0$, and denote $w_i = \tilde{\pi}_i(w)$, for $i=1,2$. We can assume that one of the following three possibilities holds:

\begin{enumerate}[label={\rm{(\alph*)}}]
    \item \label{it:ex41} $\<w_1 ,w_1\> = -1$ and $\<w_2 ,w_2\> = 1$;
    \item \label{it:ex42} $\<w_1 ,w_1\> = 1$ and $\<w_2 ,w_2\> = -1$;
    \item \label{it:ex43} $\<w_1 ,w_1\> = 0=\<w_2 ,w_2\>$,
\end{enumerate}
In cases \ref{it:ex41} and \ref{it:ex42}, let $\mathbb{R}^{n+1,1} = \operatorname{Span}(w_1,w_2)^\perp$, and let $\iota\colon \overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa) \to \mathbb{R}^{n+1,1}$ be an isometric embedding of the hyperbolic space $\overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)$ into $\mathbb{R}^{n+1,1}$ such that $ \<\iota(p),\iota(p)\>~=~\kappa^{-1}$. Define the embedding $\phi\colon\overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa) \to \mathbb{R}^{n+3,2}$ by $\phi(p) = \iota(p) + \upsilon(p) w$ for $p \in \overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)$, where the function $\upsilon\colon \overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)\to \mathbb{R}$ will be specified later. Note that $w \in \operatorname{Span}(w, \iota(p))^\perp$, for all $p \in \overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)$, by construction. 

  We have $\<\phi(p),\phi(p)\> = \<\iota(p),\iota(p)\> = \kappa^{-1}$, and so $\phi(\overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)) \subset \overline{M}^{n+2,1}(\kappa)$. Moreover, since $\<w,w\>=0$ and $w$ is orthogonal to $\iota(p)$, the embedding $\phi$ is an isometry. To ensure that $\phi(\overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)) \subset \overline{M}^{k,0}(\kappa_1)\times\overline{M}^{n-k+1,0}(\kappa_2)$, we choose the function $\upsilon\colon\overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa) \to \mathbb{R}$ in the definition of $\phi$ as follows. In case \ref{it:ex41}, define
  \[
  \upsilon(p)= (\kappa_2^{-1}-\<\tilde{\pi}_2 (\iota(p)),\tilde{\pi}_2 (\iota(p))\>)^{1/2},
  \]
  so that  $\<\tilde{\pi}_2 (\phi(p)),\tilde{\pi}_2 (\phi(p))\> = \kappa_2^{-1}$. 
  Note that $\<\tilde{\pi}_1 (\iota(p)),\tilde{\pi}_1 (\iota(p))\>\ge0$, hence
  $$\<\tilde{\pi}_2 (\iota(p)),\tilde{\pi}_2 (\iota(p))\> \le \<\iota(p),\iota(p)\> = \kappa^{-1}= \kappa_1^{-1}+\kappa_2^{-1} < \kappa_2^{-1},$$ so that $\phi$ is well defined. 
  In case \ref{it:ex42}, define
   \[
  \upsilon(p)= (\<\tilde{\pi}_2 (\iota(p)),\tilde{\pi}_2 (\iota(p))\>-\kappa_2^{-1})^{1/2},
  \]
  so that 
  $\<\tilde{\pi}_2 (\phi(p)),\tilde{\pi}_2 (\phi(p))\>= \kappa_2^{-1}$. As
 $\<\tilde{\pi}_2(\iota(p)),\tilde{\pi}_2(\iota(p))\>\geq 0$, it follows that
 $$\<\tilde{\pi}_2 (\iota(p)),\tilde{\pi}_2 (\iota(p))\>-\kappa_2^{-1}>0,$$ which shows that the map $\phi$ is well defined.

Now we consider case \ref{it:ex43}. Since $\<w_1 ,w_1\> = \<w_2 ,w_2\> = 0$,  the subspace $w^\perp \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+3,2}$ has degeneracy $1$ and index $1$.
Take any nondegenerate hyperplane $\mathbb{R}^{n+1,1} \subset w^\perp$, and define an isometric embedding $\iota\colon\overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa) \to \mathbb{R}^{n+1,1}$ in such a way that $\<\iota(p),\iota(p)\> = \kappa^{-1}$. Now define the embedding $\phi\colon \overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa) \to \mathbb{R}^{n+3,2}$ by $\phi(p) = \iota(p) + \upsilon(p) w$ for $p \in \overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)$, where we specify the function $\upsilon\colon \overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa) \to \mathbb{R}$ a little later. Again,  $w\in \operatorname{Span}( w, \iota(p))^\perp$, for all $p \in \overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)$, by construction, and so $\phi$ is an isometric embedding. Moreover, $\<\phi(p),\phi(p)\>=\<\iota(p),\iota(p)\> =\kappa^{-1}$, hence $\phi(\overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)) \subset \overline{M}^{n+2,1}(\kappa)$. Therefore, to have $\phi(\overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)) \subset \overline{M}^{k,0}(\kappa_1) \times \overline{M}^{n-k+1,0}(\kappa_2)$, we need to choose the function $\upsilon\colon \overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa) \to \mathbb{R}$ in the definition of $\phi$ in such a way that $\<\tilde{\pi}_2(\phi(p)), \tilde{\pi}_2(\phi(p))\>= \kappa_2^{-1}$, which gives 
\begin{equation*}
  \upsilon(p) = \tfrac12 \<\tilde{\pi}_2(\iota(p)), w_2\>^{-1} (\kappa_2^{-1} - \<\tilde{\pi}_2(\iota(p)), \tilde{\pi}_2(\iota(p))\>).
\end{equation*}
Note that the right-hand side is well defined. Indeed, suppose  $\<\tilde{\pi}_2(\iota(p)), w_2\>=0$ for some $p \in \overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)$. Since $w_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{n-k+2,1}$ is light-like, this implies that $\<\tilde{\pi}_2(\iota(p)), \tilde{\pi}_2(\iota(p))\> \ge 0$. But as $\<\iota(p), w\>=0$, we also have $\<\tilde{\pi}_1(\iota(p)), w_1\>=0$, hence $\<\tilde{\pi}_1(\iota(p)), \tilde{\pi}_1(\iota(p))\> \ge 0$, which contradicts the fact that $\<\iota(p),\iota(p)\> = \kappa^{-1} < 0$. Note that, also in this case, 
 $$\phi(\overline{M}^{n,0}(\kappa)) =(\overline{M}^{k,0}(\kappa_1) \times \overline{M}^{n-k+1,0}(\kappa_2))\cap w^\perp \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+3,2}.$$

label: prop:scale
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:scale}
  The metric induced by $f'$ on $M^3$ from $\< \cdot, \cdot \>'$  has constant sectional curvature $\kappa=\frac{\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}$, and the shape operator of $f'$ also has rank $2$.
head: environment

label: eq:newbasis
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $(E_1', E_2', E_3')$ be the frame on $M^3$ defined by  \begin{equation}\label{eq:newbasis}
        E_1' = R_1^{-1} E_1, \quad E_2' = R_2^{-1} E_2, \quad E_3' =\sqrt{2} R^{-1} \, E_3.
        \end{equation}
        Since $t=1-r=1/2$, the vector field  $\zeta$ defined by \eqref{zeta} is $\zeta=\frac{1}{2}E_3$ by the last two equations in \eqref{propR}. Therefore, \eqref{R} and \eqref{R2} give 
        $\pi_i^*f'_*E'_j=\delta_{ij}R_j^{-1}f'_*E_j$
 for $1\leq i,j\leq 2$, and 
$\pi_j^*f'_*E_3'=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}R^{-1}(f'_*E_3+\xi)$ for $j=1,2$. Since $R^2=R_1^2+R_2^2$, it follows from \eqref{eq:ip'} that $(E_1', E_2', E_3')$ is an orthonormal frame with respect to $\< \cdot, \cdot \>'$.  Moreover, using that
$\pi_j^*\xi=\frac{1}{2}((-1)^{j}f'_*E_3+\xi)$ for $j=1,2$ by \eqref{zeta} and \eqref{zeta2}, it follows from \eqref{eq:ip'} that
\begin{equation}\label{N}
        \xi' = \sqrt{2} R^{-1} (R_1^{-1}R_2 \pi_1^* \xi + R_2^{-1}R_1 \pi_2^* \xi)
  \end{equation}
  is a unit normal vector field along $f'$.
  Furthermore, the integral curves of the vector field $E_3'$ are the same as the integral curves of the vector field $E_3$, and as such, are geodesics of $M^3$ and are mapped by $f'$ into geodesics of $\overline{M}_1^2(\kappa_1)\times\overline{M}_2^{2}(\kappa_2)$ (since a geodesic in a Riemannian product remains such when we homothetically scale the metrics on the factors).

  The components of the shape operator $S'$ of $f'$ are given by $S'_{ij} = \<\nabla^0_{E_i'} f'_*E_j', \xi'\>'$ for $i,j=1,2,3$ (recall that the Levi-Civita connections of $\< \cdot, \cdot \>$ and of $\< \cdot, \cdot \>'$ coincide). We already know that $S'_{33}=0$. We compute the remaining components using~\eqref{eq:Aij'}, \eqref{eq:ip'} and \eqref{eq:newbasis}:
  \begin{align*}
    S'_{11} & = \<\nabla^0_{E_1'} f'_*E_1', \xi'\>' = R_1^{-2} \<\nabla^0_{E_1} f'_*E_1, \xi'\>' = R_1^{-2} \<\nabla^0_{E_1} f'_*E_1, \pi_1^* \xi'\>' = \<\nabla^0_{E_1} f'_*E_1, \pi_1^* \xi'\> \\
    &= \sqrt{2} R^{-1} R_1^{-1}R_2 \<\nabla^0_{E_1} f'_*E_1, \pi_1^* \xi\> = \sqrt{2} R^{-1} R_1^{-1}R_2 \<\nabla^0_{E_1} f'_*E_1, \xi\> = \sqrt{2} R^{-1}R_1^{-1}R_2 S_{11}, \\
    S'_{21} & = \<\nabla^0_{E_2'} f'_*E_1', \xi'\>' = R_1^{-1} R_2^{-1} \<\nabla^0_{E_2} f'_*E_1, \xi'\>' = R_1^{-1} R_2^{-1} \<\nabla^0_{E_2} f'_*E_1, \pi_1^* \xi'\>'\\& = R_2^{-1}R_1\<\nabla^0_{E_2} f'_*E_1, \pi_1^* \xi'\> 
    = \sqrt{2} R^{-1} \<\nabla^0_{E_2} f'_*E_1, \pi_1^* \xi\> = \sqrt{2} R^{-1} \<\nabla^0_{E_2} f'_*E_1, \xi\>\\& = \sqrt{2} R^{-1} S_{21},\\
    S'_{22} & = \<\nabla^0_{E_2'} f'_*E_2', \xi'\>' = R_2^{-2} \<\nabla^0_{E_2} f'_*E_2, \xi'\>' = R_2^{-2} \<\nabla^0_{E_2} f'_*E_2, \pi_2^* \xi'\>' = \<\nabla^0_{E_2} f'_*E_2, \pi_2^* \xi'\> \\
    &= \sqrt{2} R^{-1} R_2^{-1}R_1 \<\nabla^0_{E_2} f'_*E_2, \pi_2^* \xi\> = \sqrt{2} R^{-1} R_2^{-1}R_1 \<\nabla^0_{E_2} f'_*E_2, \xi\> = \sqrt{2} R^{-1} R_2^{-1}R_1 S_{22}, \\
    S'_{31} & = \<\nabla^0_{E_3'} f'_*E_1', \xi'\>' = \sqrt{2} R^{-1} R_1^{-1} \<\nabla^0_{E_3} f'_*E_1, \xi'\>' = \sqrt{2} R^{-1} R_1^{-1} \<\nabla^0_{E_3} f'_*E_1, \pi_1^* \xi'\>' \\
    &= \sqrt{2} R^{-1} R_1\<\nabla^0_{E_3}f'_*E_1, \pi_1^* \xi'\> = 2 R^{-2} R_2 \<\nabla^0_{E_3} f'_*E_1, \pi_1^* \xi\> = 2 R^{-2} R_1 \<\nabla^0_{E_3} f'_*E_1, \xi\> = 0,\\
    S'_{32} & = \<\nabla^0_{E_3'} f'_*E_2', \xi'\>' = \sqrt{2} R^{-1} R_2^{-1} \<\nabla^0_{E_3} f'_*E_2, \xi'\>' =\sqrt{2} R^{-1} R_2^{-1} \<\nabla^0_{E_3} f'_*E_2, \pi_2^* \xi'\>' \\
    &= \sqrt{2} R^{-1} R_2\<\nabla^0_{E_3} f'_*E_2, \pi_2^* \xi'\> = 2 R^{-2} R_1 \<\nabla^0_{E_3} f'_*E_2, \pi_1^* \xi\> = 2 R^{-2} R_1\<\nabla^0_{E_3} f'_*E_2, \xi\> = 0.
  \end{align*}

  It follows that $E_3'$ lies in the kernel of $S'$, and $S'_{11} S'_{22} - (S'_{12})^2 =  2 R^{-2} (S_{11} S_{22} - S_{12}^2)=\varepsilon R^{-2}=\kappa$, by~\eqref{eq:Aij'}.  Hence $\operatorname{rk} S' = 2$. Moreover, from Gauss equation, the only nonzero components of the curvature tensor $R'$ of $M^3$, up to $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetries, are
  \begin{align*}
  R'(E_1',E_2',E_2',E_1') & = \kappa, \\
  R'(E_1',E_3',E_3',E_1') & = \kappa_1\<\pi_1^*f'_*E_3',\pi_1^*f'_*E_3'\>' = 2\kappa_1R_1^2R^{-2} \<\pi_1^*f'_*E_3,\pi_1^*f'_*E_3\> = \varepsilon R^{-2}=\kappa,\\
  R'(E_2',E_3',E_3',E_2') & = \kappa_2\<\pi_2^*f'_*E_3',\pi_2^*f'_*E_3'\>' = 2\kappa_2R_2^2R^{-2}  \<\pi_2^*f'_*E_3,\pi_2^*f'_*E_3\> = \varepsilon R^{-2}=\kappa,
  \end{align*}
  by \eqref{eq:ip'} and \eqref{eq:newbasis}. This completes the proof.

title: Remark
body_md:
Hypersurfaces of $\overline{M}^2(\varepsilon)\times\overline{M}^{2}(\varepsilon)$, $\varepsilon\in \{-1, 1\}$, with constant sectional curvature and $\operatorname{rk} S=2$ satisfying  $S\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{R} S$, correspond to \cite[Theorem~1.1(1)]{LVWY} for $\varepsilon=1$, and to \cite[Theorem~1.1(2)]{LVWYhyp} for $\varepsilon=-1$, in the classification of all hypersurfaces with constant sectional curvature of 
$\overline{M}^2(\varepsilon)\times\overline{M}^{2}(\varepsilon)$.  
The case of hypersurfaces with constant sectional curvature and $\operatorname{rk} S =2$ for which  $S\mathcal{R}\neq  \mathcal{R} S$ correspond to \cite[Theorem~1.1(2)]{LVWY} for $\varepsilon=1$ and to \cite[Theorem~1.1(3)]{LVWYhyp} for $\varepsilon=-1$. More precisely, it was shown in \cite{LVWY} that any hypersurface
$f\colon M^3(1/2)\to\mathbb{S}^2\times \mathbb{S}^2$ with $\operatorname{rk} S = 2$ for which $S\mathcal{R}\neq \mathcal{R} S$ is a parallel hypersurface at a distance $\tfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}$ of a minimal hypersurface of $\mathbb{S}^2\times \mathbb{S}^2$ with vanishing product angle function, and such minimal hypersurfaces were described in Theorem 3.5 of that paper. On the other hand, hypersurfaces
$f\colon M^3(-1/2)\to\mathbb{H}^2\times \mathbb{H}^2$ with $\operatorname{rk} S = 2$ for which $S\mathcal{R}\neq \mathcal{R} S$ were described in \cite[Theorems 5.7--5.10]{LVWYhyp}. In either case, $f$ has a vanishing product angle function.

title: Proof
body_md:
We use the notation of Section~\ref{sec:hypprod}.
We first dispose of the case $\operatorname{rk} S\le 1$, which is ruled out by Lemma~\ref{lem:rks01}.
The cases $\kappa_1\kappa_2=0$ are already covered in \cite{MaT} and \cite{CT}, as stated in 
items~\ref{it:thm11} and~\ref{it:thm12}. 

Henceforth, we assume that $\kappa_1\kappa_2\ne0$ and $2\le k\le n-1$. 

 Let $\xi$ be a unit normal vector field along $f$, and let
    $
    h\colon \overline{M}^{k}(\kappa_1)\times\overline{M}^{n-k+1}(\kappa_2) \to \mathbb{R}^{k+1,\sigma(\kappa_1)}\times \mathbb{R}^{n-k+2,\sigma(\kappa_2)} = \mathbb{R}^{n+3,\eta}
    $
    be the inclusion, where $\eta = \sigma(\kappa_1)+\sigma(\kappa_2)$. Then
    \[
    h(\overline{M}^{k}(\kappa_1)\times\overline{M}^{n-k+1}(\kappa_2)) \subset \overline{M}^{n+2,\rho}(\tilde{\kappa}),\quad \tilde{\kappa} = \frac{\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2},
    \]
    where
   $$
 \rho=\eta - \sigma(\tilde{\kappa})=\left\{ \begin{array}{l} 0, \,\,\,\mbox{if}\,\,\, \kappa_1, \kappa_2>0,\,\,\,\mbox{or} \,\,\, \kappa_1\kappa_2<0\,\,\,\mbox{and}\,\,\,
 \kappa_1+\kappa_2>0,\\
 1,\,\,\,\mbox{if}\,\,\, \kappa_1, \kappa_2<0,\,\,\,\mbox{or} \,\,\,\kappa_1 \kappa_2<0\,\,\,\mbox{and}\,\,\, \kappa_1+\kappa_2<0.\\
 \end{array}\right.
 $$
 Denote $i\colon\overline{M}^{k}(\kappa_1)\times\overline{M}^{n-k+1}(\kappa_2) \to \overline{M}^{n+2,\rho}(\tilde{\kappa})\subset \mathbb{R}^{n+3,\eta}$ the inclusion, and let $\tilde{f} = i\circ f$. Define 
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:UV}
     U =-|\tilde \kappa|^{1/2}(R_1\nu_1+R_2\nu_2)\,\,\,\,\mbox{and}\,\,\,\,V=|\tilde \kappa|^{1/2}(-\varepsilon_1R_2\nu_1+\varepsilon_2R_1\nu_2).
 \end{equation}
It follows from \eqref{eq:nu} and \eqref{eq:nu'} that 
$$S_U=|\tilde \kappa|^{1/2}\,I\,\,\,\,\mbox{and}\,\,\,\,S_V=aI+b\mathcal{R},$$
  with
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:ab} a=|\tilde\kappa|^{1/2}\frac{R_2}{\varepsilon_1R_1}=\frac{\kappa_1}{|\kappa_1+\kappa_2|^{1/2}}\,\,\,\,\mbox{and}\,\,\,\,b=-|\tilde\kappa|^{1/2}\frac{\varepsilon_2R_1^2+\varepsilon_1R_2^2}{R_1R_2}=
 -\frac{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}{|\kappa_1+\kappa_2|^{1/2}}.
 \end{equation}
 Thus, $U$ is normal to $\overline{M}^{n+2,\rho}(\tilde\kappa)$ along $\tilde{F}=h\circ f$, and $\{i_*\xi,V\}$ is an orthonormal frame of the normal space $N_{\tilde{f}}M^n$.
 
We start with the following fact.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:setcons}
    In the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{mainthmb}, with $\kappa_1\kappa_2\ne0$ and $2\le k\le n-1$, the following holds.
    \begin{enumerate}[label={\rm{(\alph*)}}]
        \item\label{it:setcons1} If $n\ge 4$ or $n=\operatorname{rk} S=3$, then  $\kappa_1 \kappa_2<0$, with $\kappa_1+\kappa_2<0$, or $\kappa_1, \kappa_2<0$. 
        \item\label{it:setcons2} If $n=3$ and $\operatorname{rk} S=2$, then $\kappa_1\kappa_2>0$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Moreover, in both cases, $\kappa=\frac{\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
   For assertion~\ref{it:setcons1}, we first suppose that $n\ge 4$ and $\kappa\ne\tilde\kappa$. Let $j\colon\overline{M}^{n+2,\rho}(\tilde\kappa)\to \overline{M}^{n+3,\delta}(\kappa)$ be an umbilical isometric immersion, where  $\delta=\rho$ if $\tilde\kappa > \kappa$ and  $\delta=\rho+1$ if $\tilde\kappa < \kappa$. Let $F=j\circ \tilde f$. Then the second fundamental form $\mathrm{II}_{F}(x)$ of $F$ at any $x\in M^n$ is flat with respect to the inner product in the normal space $N_{F}M^n(x)$, which has index
 $$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} 0, \,\,\,\mbox{if either}\,\,\, \kappa_1, \kappa_2>0,\,\,\mbox{or}
 \,\,\, \kappa_1\kappa_2<0,\,\kappa_1+\kappa_2>0\,\,\,\mbox{and}\,\,\,\tilde\kappa > \kappa,\\
 2,  \,\,\,\mbox{if either}\,\,\,\kappa_1, \kappa_2<0\,\,\mbox{and}\,\, \tilde\kappa < \kappa,\,\,\mbox{or}
 \,\,\, \kappa_1\kappa_2<0,\, \kappa_1+\kappa_2<0\,\,\,\mbox{and} \,\,\tilde\kappa < \kappa,\\
 1, \,\,\,\mbox{in the remaining cases}.
 \end{array}\right.$$
  Notice that the inner product in the (one-dimensional) normal space to $j$ at $x$ is positive definite if $\tilde\kappa > \kappa$ and negative definite otherwise. Let $\nu$ be one of the two normal vectors to $j$ at $x$ such that $\<\nu, \nu\>=(\tilde\kappa - \kappa)/|\tilde\kappa - \kappa|$ and 
  $S_\nu= \sqrt{|\tilde\kappa - \kappa|}\,I$. In particular, the latter equation implies that $\mathrm{II}_F(x)$ has a trivial kernel.    
  
 The case in which the inner product on $N_F M^n(x)$ is positive definite is then ruled out by Lemma~\ref{lem:flatbi}\eqref{it:pode},
 which implies that $0=\dim \mathcal{N}(\mathrm{II}_{F}(x))\geq n-3$, in contradiction with the assumption that $n\geq 4$. 
 Multiplying by $-1$ the inner product on $N_FM^n(x)$ if it has index~$2$, it becomes a Lorentzian inner product. 
  Therefore, in the cases in which the inner product on $N_FM^n(x)$ has index either $1$ or $2$, Lemma~\ref{lem:flatbi}\eqref{it:symim} implies that the subspace $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_F(x))$ spanned by the image of $\mathrm{II}_F(x)$ must be degenerate for every $x\in M^n$, for otherwise we would reach the same contradiction as in the positive definite case. 

  Thus, there exists a nonzero vector $N\in \mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_F(x))\cap (\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_F(x)))^\perp$. Observe that $N$ cannot be orthogonal to $\nu$, as otherwise $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x))$ would be a degenerate subspace of a Lorentzian plane, and hence would be spanned by a light-like vector. This would imply that $\kappa =\tilde\kappa$ from Gauss equation of $\tilde f$, a contradiction. Consequently, we may assume that $N=i_*N_1+\nu$ for some $N_1 \in N_{\tilde{f}}M^n(x)$ with $\<N_1,N_1\> = \varepsilon = -(\tilde\kappa - \kappa)/|\tilde\kappa - \kappa|$. Since
    $$0=\<\mathrm{II}_{F}(X, Y), N\>=\<i_*\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(X, Y)+ \sqrt{|\tilde\kappa-\kappa|}\<X, Y\>\nu, i_*N_1+\nu\>,$$
    it follows that $S_{N_1} = \varepsilon\sqrt{|\tilde\kappa - \kappa|}I$.
    Choosing $N_2 \in N_{\tilde{f}}M^n(x)$ orthogonal to $N_1$ with $\<N_2,N_2\> = -\varepsilon$, Gauss equation of $\tilde{f}$ implies that $\operatorname{rk} S_{N_2} \le 1$. Therefore, $\{N_1,N_2\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $N_{\tilde{f}}M^n(x)$ such that
     $$S_{N_1}=\varepsilon \sqrt{|\tilde\kappa - \kappa|}\,I\,\,\,\mbox{and}\,\,\operatorname{rk} S_{N_2}\le 1.$$
    Now let $\theta \in C^\infty(M^n)$ be such that 
     $$i_*\xi=\cos \theta N_1+\sin \theta N_2 \,\,\,\,\mbox{and}\,\,\,\,V=-\sin\theta N_1+\cos\theta N_2.$$ 
     Then, on $\ker S_{N_2}$ we have
      $$S=\varepsilon\sqrt{|\tilde\kappa - \kappa|}\cos\theta\,I\,\,\, \mbox{and}\,\,\, aI+b\mathcal{R}=-\varepsilon\sqrt{|\tilde\kappa - \kappa|}\sin\theta\,I.$$
      Since $\dim\ker S_{N_2} \ge n-1$, it follows from the second of the above equations that $\mathcal{R}$ can have at most two distinct eigenvalues. As $\dim\ker\mathcal{R} \ge k-1 \ge 1$ and $\dim\ker(I-\mathcal{R})\ge n-k \ge 1$ by \eqref{dimkerR} and our assumption that $2\leq k\leq n-1$, such eigenvalues must be $0$ and $1$, with multiplicities  $(n-1, 1)$ or $(1, n-1)$. It follows from \eqref{dimkerR} that $k=n-1$ in the former case and $k=2$ in the latter. Moreover, $f$ is locally decomposable by Proposition~\ref{splits}; in particular, $\kappa=0$. But since both factors have dimensions greater than one and one of them is an inclusion,
     this leads to a contradiction.

     Now we have $\kappa=\tilde\kappa=\frac{\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}$. Then, at any $x\in M^n$, the second fundamental form $\mathrm{II}_{\tilde{f}}(x)$ is a flat bilinear form with respect to the inner product on $N_{\tilde{f}}M^n(x)$, whose index is equal to $\rho$. Therefore, if $\rho=0$, then $\dim\mathcal{N}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x)) \ge n-2$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:flatbi}\eqref{it:pode}.
     On the subspace $\mathcal{N}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f})$ at $x\in M^n$, we have $S=0=aI+b\mathcal{R}$. Since $-ab^{-1}=\kappa_1(\kappa_1+ \kappa_2)^{-1}$, by the assumption that $n\geq 4$ this contradicts the fact that the eigenvalues of $\mathcal{R}$ lie in $[0,1]$ and that the unique eigenvalue of $\mathcal{R}$ in $(0,1)$ has multiplicity one.
     Thus, we must have $\rho=1$, hence  $\kappa_1 \kappa_2<0$, with $\kappa_1+\kappa_2<0$, or $\kappa_1, \kappa_2<0$. 


     Next, when $n=\operatorname{rk} S=3$, the claim follows from \cite[Lemma~6(a)]{KNT}.

     We now prove assertion~\ref{it:setcons2}. Suppose that $n=3$ and $\operatorname{rk} S=2$. Arguing by contradiction, assume $\kappa\ne\tilde\kappa$. Then the same argument as in the case $n\ge 4$ applies, except that we must also consider the case in which the inner product on $N_{F}M^3(x)$ at a point $x\in M^3$ is positive definite. But then, since $\mathrm{II}_{F}(x)$ has trivial kernel, $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{F}(x))=N_{F}M^3(x)$. It follows from \cite[Theorem~5.2]{DT} that there exists a frame $\{X_1,X_2,X_3\}$ that diagonalises $\mathrm{II}_{F}$. As $S_{\nu}=\sqrt{|\tilde\kappa-\kappa|}I$, such a frame is orthogonal; hence, it may be chosen as an orthonormal frame. In particular, this frame diagonalises $\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}$ and so diagonalises $S$ and $aI+b\mathcal{R}$, thus $S\mathcal{R} = \mathcal{R} S$. We take $X_2=\|\zeta\|^{-1}\zeta$, then we obtain
     \begin{gather*}
         SX_1=\lambda_1 X_1,\quad SX_2=\lambda_2 X_2,\quad SX_3=\lambda_3 X_3,\\
         \mathcal{R} X_1 = 0,\quad \mathcal{R} X_2 = r X_2, \quad \mathcal{R} X_3 = X_3,\\
         (I-\mathcal{R})X_1 = X_1,\quad (I-\mathcal{R})X_2 = (1-r)X_2,\quad (I-\mathcal{R})X_3 = 0.
     \end{gather*}
     Gauss equation~\eqref{Gauss} gives $\kappa=\lambda_1\lambda_2 + \kappa_1(1-r)  = \lambda_2\lambda_3+\kappa_2 r = \lambda_1\lambda_3$. This yields $\lambda_1\lambda_3\ne 0$ and so $\lambda_2=0$ as $\operatorname{rk} S =2$. Moreover, we have $\kappa_1(1-r)=\kappa=\kappa_2 r$, which implies $\kappa=\frac{\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}=\tilde\kappa$, a contradiction. 
     
     Now we have $\kappa=\frac{\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}$. Then, $\mathrm{II}_{\tilde{f}}(x)$ is a flat bilinear form for every $x\in M^3$, and hence it has nontrivial kernel by Lemma~\ref{lem:flatbi}\eqref{it:pode}. In particular, $S_{V} = aI + b\mathcal{R}$ has nontrivial kernel and $r=-ab^{-1} = \kappa_1(\kappa_1+\kappa_2)^{-1}$. Since $\mathcal{N}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}) = \ker S \cap \ker S_V$, a vector field $Y$ spanning $\mathcal{N}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f})$ satisfies $SY= 0 $ and $\mathcal{R} Y = rY$. Computing the sectional curvatures of the planes spanned by $\{X,Y\}$ and $\{Y,Z\}$, where $\{X,Y,Z\}$ is an orthonormal frame such that $\mathcal{R} X = 0$ and $\mathcal{R} Z= Z$, and using Gauss equation of $F$, we have $\kappa_1(1-r)=\kappa=\kappa_2 r$, which implies $\kappa_1\kappa_2>0$.
\end{proof}



The proof of the theorem is divided into three cases: $n\ge 4$, $n=\operatorname{rk} S=3$, and $n=3$ with $\operatorname{rk} S=2$. 

\vspace{1ex}

\underline{Case 1. $n\ge 4$}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:setcons}\ref{it:setcons1}, we have $\kappa=\frac{\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}$, with $\kappa_1+\kappa_2<0$.


    
     If $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x))$ was nondegenerate, we would reach the contradiction using Lemma~\ref{lem:flatbi}\eqref{it:symim}. 
     As a result, $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x))$ is degenerate for any $x\in M^n$.  This means that, for all $x\in M^n$ and all $X, Y\in T_xM^n$,
 $$0=\<\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(X,Y), i_*\xi+V\>=\<SX, Y\>-\<(aI+b\mathcal{R})X, Y\>,$$
 hence  $S=aI+b\mathcal{R}$ (and in particular $S\mathcal{R} = \mathcal{R} S$).

  \begin{eqnarray*}
  \mathrm{II}_{\tilde F}(X,Y)&=&h_*\mathrm{II}_f(X,Y) -\frac{1}{R_1}\<(I-\mathcal{R})X, Y\> \nu_1+\frac{1}{R_2}\<\mathcal{R} X, Y\>
    \nu_2\\
    &=& \<(aI+b\mathcal{R})X, Y\>h_*\xi -\frac{1}{R_1}\<(I-\mathcal{R})X, Y\> \nu_1+\frac{1}{R_2}\<\mathcal{R} X, Y\>\nu_2\\
    &=& \<X, Y\>\left(a h_*\xi-\frac{1}{R_1}\nu_1\right)+\<\mathcal{R} X,Y\>\left(b h_*\xi+\frac{1}{R_1}\nu_1+\frac{1}{R_2}\nu_2\right),
    \end{eqnarray*}
  where $\kappa_1=R_1^{-2}$ and $\kappa_2=-R_2^{-2}$.
  Thus the first normal space $N^1_{\tilde F}M^n(x)$ of $\tilde{F}$ at any $x\in M^n$ is spanned by the vectors $ah_*\xi-\frac{1}{R_1}\nu_1$ and $bh_*\xi+\frac{1}{R_1}\nu_1+\frac{1}{R_2}\nu_2$, or equivalently, using~\eqref{eq:ab},
   by the vectors 
   $$Z_1=\kappa^{1/2}R_2 h_*\xi -\nu_1\,\,\,\mbox{and}\,\,\,Z_2=\kappa^{-1/2}h_*\xi + R_2\nu_1+R_1\nu_2.$$
   Notice that $Z_2\in (\operatorname{Span}(Z_1, Z_2))^\perp,$ hence $\operatorname{Span}(Z_1, Z_2)$ is a degenerate vector subbundle of rank two. Now we have, for any $X\in\Gamma(TM^n)$,
 \begin{eqnarray*}
 \nabla_X^\perp h_*\xi&=&\mathrm{II}_h(f_*X,h_*\xi)\\
 &=&-\frac{1}{R_1}\<\tilde \pi_1 \xi,f_*X\> \nu_1+\frac{1}{R_2}\<\tilde \pi_2 \xi,f_*X\>\nu_2\\
 &=&\<X, \zeta\>\left(\frac{1}{R_1}\nu_1+\frac{1}{R_2}\nu_2\right),
 \end{eqnarray*}
 $$\nabla_X^\perp\nu_1=-\frac{1}{R_1}\<X,\zeta\>h_*\xi\,\,\,\,\mbox{and}\,\,\,\,\nabla_X^\perp\nu_2=\frac{1}{R_2}\<X,\zeta\>h_*\xi.$$
 Thus,
  $$
 \begin{array}{l}
 \nabla_X^\perp Z_2=\kappa^{-1/2}\<X, \zeta\>\left(\frac{1}{R_1}\nu_1+\frac{1}{R_2}\nu_2\right)-\frac{R_2}{R_1}\<X,\zeta\>h_*\xi+\frac{R_1}{R_2}\<X,\zeta\>h_*\xi\vspace{2ex}\\
 \hspace*{7ex}= \frac{\kappa^{-1/2}}{R_1R_2}\<X,\zeta\> Z_2.
 \end{array}
 $$
  Observe that, by Lemma~\ref{lem:grad}, the vector field $\zeta$ is a gradient vector field. 
  Taking (locally) a positive $\lambda\in C^{\infty}(M^n)$ such that 
 $\mbox{grad\,}(\log\lambda)=-\frac{\kappa^{-1/2}}{R_1R_2} \zeta$ implies that $w=\lambda Z_2$ is a constant vector in $\mathbb{R}^{n+3,1}$, for $Z_2\in \Gamma((N_{\tilde F}^{1}M^n)^\perp)$ and
 $$\nabla_X^\perp \lambda Z_2=X(\lambda)Z_2+\lambda \nabla_X^\perp Z_2=\left(\<\mbox{grad\,} \lambda, X\>+\frac{ \kappa^{-1/2}}{R_1R_2}\lambda\<X,\zeta\>\right)Z_2=0.$$
 Therefore  $\tilde F(M^n)$ is contained in the intersection of $\overline{M}^{k}(\kappa_1)\times \overline{M}^{n-k+1}(\kappa_2)\subset \mathbb{R}^{n+3,1}$ with a degenerate hyperplane $\mathcal{H}$ orthogonal to $w$. Since $w$ is orthogonal to $U$, which is a multiple of the position vector of $\tilde F$, then $\mathcal{H}$ passes through the origin. This proves the statement~\ref{it:thm13} when $\kappa_1\kappa_2<0$.  

  We now suppose that $\kappa_1, \kappa_2<0$, say, $\kappa_1=-R_1^{-2}$ and $\kappa_2=-R_2^{-2}$.
  Then an argument analogous to that used in the case $\kappa_1\kappa_2<0$ shows that the first normal space $N_{\tilde{F}}^{1}M^n(x)$ at any $x\in M^n$ is spanned by the vectors
  $$Y_1=-|\kappa|^{1/2}R_2h_*\xi+\nu_1\,\,\,\mbox{and}\,\,\,Y_2=|\kappa|^{-1/2}h_*\xi-R_2\nu_1+R_1\nu_2$$ and forms a degenerate vector subbundle of rank two, for $Y_2\in (N_{\tilde{F}}^{1}M^n(x))^\perp$. Using that $\nabla_X^{\perp}Y_2 = \frac{|\kappa|^{-1/2}}{R_1R_2}\<X,\zeta\> Y_2$, one shows as in the previous case that there exists a  positive $\mu\in C^\infty(M^n)$ such that $\nabla_X^\perp \mu Y_2=0$, which, together with the fact that $Y_2\in (N_{\tilde{F}}^{1}M^n(x))^\perp$, implies that $w=\mu Y_2$ is a constant vector  in $\mathbb{R}^{n+3,2}$. It follows that $\tilde{F}(M^n)$ is contained in the intersection of $\overline{M}^{k}(\kappa_1)\times \overline{M}^{n-k+1}(\kappa_2)\subset \mathbb{R}^{n+3,2}$ with a degenerate hyperplane $\mathcal{H}$ orthogonal to $w$. As before, the fact that $w$ is orthogonal to $U$, which is a multiple of the position vector of $\tilde F$, implies that $\mathcal{H}$ passes through the origin, thereby proving that $f(M^n)$ is as stated in~\ref{it:thm13} when $\kappa_1, \kappa_2<0$.

  
\vspace{1ex}


\underline{Case 2. $n=\operatorname{rk} S=3$}.
We have $\kappa_1+\kappa_2< 0$ and  $\kappa=\frac{\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:setcons}\ref{it:setcons1}. 
   

At each point $x\in M^3(\kappa)$, the second fundamental form $\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x)$ is a flat bilinear form with respect to the Lorentzian inner product on $N_{\tilde f}M^3(x)$. Hence, if $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x))$ was nondegenerate,  by Lemma~\ref{lem:flatbi}\eqref{it:pode} 
the index of relative nullity of $\tilde f$ at $x$ would be at least~$1$, contradicting our assumption that $\operatorname{rk} S=3$. Therefore, $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x))$ must be degenerate for all $x\in M^3(\kappa)$. Consequently,
 $$0=\<\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(X,Y), i_*\xi + V\>=\<SX, Y\>-\<(aI+b\mathcal{R})X, Y\>$$
 for all $X,Y\in \Gamma(TM^3)$, which shows that $S=aI+b\mathcal{R}$. 

 Now, in either of the possible cases $\kappa_1\kappa_2<0$ (with $\kappa_2<0<\kappa_1$), or $\kappa_1,\kappa_2<0$, one may argue as in the proof of the case $n\geq 4$ to conclude that the assertion \ref{it:thm13} in the statement holds. 



\vspace{1ex}

\underline{Case 3. $n=3$ and $\operatorname{rk} S=2$}.
We have from Lemma~\ref{lem:setcons}\ref{it:setcons2} that $\kappa=\frac{\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}$, with $\kappa_1\kappa_2>0$.

Let $(E_1, E_2, E_3)$ be an orthonormal diagonalising frame of the tensor $\mathcal{R}$, with $\mathcal{R} E_1=0$, $\mathcal{R} E_2=E_2$,  and $\mathcal{R} E_3=rE_3$, where $r$  takes values in $(0,1)$.   Let $\iota\colon \overline{M}^2(\kappa_1)\times\overline{M}^2(\kappa_2)\to \overline{M}^5(\kappa)$ be the inclusion, and set $\tilde{f}=\iota\circ f$.  Then, at each point $x\in M^3(\kappa)$, $\mathrm{II}_{\tilde{f}}(x)$ is a flat bilinear form with respect to the inner product on the normal space $N_{\tilde f}M^3(x)$, which is positive definite if both $\kappa_1$  and $\kappa_2$ are positive, and Lorentzian if both are negative.   In the former case, it follows from    Lemma~\ref{lem:flatbi}\eqref{it:pode} that $\mathrm{II}_{\tilde{f}}(x)$ has nontrivial kernel.   
  Let $(U, V)$ be the orthonormal frame of $N_{\tilde f}M^3$ given by \eqref{eq:UV}, with $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon=\varepsilon_2$. Since 
  $\mathcal{N}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde{f}}(x))=\ker S\cap \ker S_V\subset \ker S$, and the latter has dimension one, it follows that

$\ker S_V=\operatorname{Span}(E_3)=\ker S$.
Therefore, 
$0=S_V E_3=(aI+b\mathcal{R}) E_3$, hence $\mathcal{R} E_3=-\frac{a}{b}E_3=\frac{\kappa_1}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}E_3$,
  and the claim is proved in this case. If both $\kappa_1$  and $\kappa_2$ are negative
  and the subspace $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x)) $ spanned by the image of $\mathrm{II}_{\tilde{f}}(x)$ is nondegenerate, the claim follows  as before using  Lemma~\ref{lem:flatbi}\eqref{it:symim}.
  On the other hand,  $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x)) $ being degenerate means that $S=S_V=aI+bR$, which can only have nontrivial kernel if $0=S_V E_3=(aI+b\mathcal{R})E_3$, hence $SE_3=0$ and $\mathcal{R} E_3=\frac{\kappa_1}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}E_3$, thus proving the claim also in this case.

  Notice that the argument in the preceding paragraph has shown that  
  $\mathcal{N}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde{f}}(x))=\operatorname{Span}(E_3)$. 
  This implies that the integral curves of $E_3$ are relative nullity leaves of $\tilde{f}$, hence they are geodesics of $M^3$ (this also follows from \eqref{derS2}), and are mapped by $\tilde{f}$ into geodesics of $\overline{M}^5(\kappa)$, in particular into geodesics of $\overline{M}^2(\kappa_1)\times \overline{M}^2(\kappa_2)$.  
  In summary, any hypersurface $f\colon M^3(\kappa)\to \overline{M}^2(\kappa_1)\times \overline{M}^2(\kappa_2)$, with $\operatorname{rk} S=2$ everywhere, satisfies the following:


\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
  \item[\textbullet]
  $\kappa = \frac{\kappa_1 \kappa_2}{\kappa_1 + \kappa_2}$, or equivalently, $ R^2 = R_1^2 + R^2_2$, where $\kappa_1=\varepsilon R_1^{-2}$,  $\kappa_2=\varepsilon R_2^{-2}$ and $\kappa=\varepsilon R^{-2}$.
    \item[\textbullet] \label{it:frame}
  The eigenfunction $r$ of $\mathcal{R}$ taking values in $(0,1)$ has the constant value $r=\frac{\kappa_1}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}$. Equivalently, the product angle function $C$ has the constant value $C=\frac{\kappa_1-\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}$. Therefore, there is an orthonormal frame $(E_1, E_2, E_3)$ on $M^3$ such that $\mathcal{R} E_1=0$, $\mathcal{R} E_2=E_2$ and 
  $\mathcal{R} E_3=\frac{\kappa_1}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}E_3$. 
  \item[\textbullet]
  The integral curves of $E_3$ are geodesics in $M^3(\kappa)$ and are mapped by $f$ into geodesics of $\overline{M}^2(\kappa_1)\times\overline{M}^{2}(\kappa_2)$.
  \item[\textbullet]
  The components $S_{ij}=\<\nabla^0_{E_i}f_*E_j, \xi\>$ of the shape operator $S$ with respect to a unit normal vector field $\xi$ (where $\nabla^0$ is the flat Levi-Civita connection of $\< \cdot, \cdot \>$ on $\mathbb{R}^{3, \varepsilon}_1 \times \mathbb{R}^{3, \varepsilon}_2$) satisfy
  \begin{equation} \label{eq:Aij}
    S_{13} = S_{23} = S_{33} = 0, \qquad  S_{11} S_{22} - S_{12}^2 = \kappa=\varepsilon R^{-2}.
  \end{equation}
\end{itemize}



Here, as in the paragraphs that precede Proposition \ref{prop:scale}, we denote each factor by the corresponding subscript, and consider the product $\overline{M}_1^2(\kappa_1)\times\overline{M}_2^{2}(\kappa_2)$ lying in the product $\mathbb{R}^{3, \varepsilon}_1 \times \mathbb{R}^{3, \varepsilon}_2$ of two mutually orthogonal Euclidean or Lorentzian spaces, according as $\varepsilon=1$ or $\varepsilon=-1$, respectively. For $i =1,2$,  $\< \cdot, \cdot \>_i$ denotes the inner product on $\mathbb{R}^{3, \varepsilon}_i$ and $\pi_i\colon \mathbb{R}^{3, \varepsilon}_1 \times \mathbb{R}^{3, \varepsilon}_2 \to \mathbb{R}^{3, \varepsilon}_i$ the corresponding orthogonal projection. As before, we again denote $\< \cdot, \cdot \>$ the inner product on $\mathbb{R}^{3, \varepsilon}_1 \times \mathbb{R}^{3, \varepsilon}_2$ defined by $\<X,Y\>= \<\pi_1 X, \pi_1 Y\>_1 + \<\pi_2 X, \pi_2 Y\>_2$, for $X, Y \in \mathbb{R}^{3, \varepsilon}_1 \times \mathbb{R}^{3, \varepsilon}_2$, and now define the new inner products $\widehat{\< \cdot, \cdot \>}_i$ on $\mathbb{R}^{3,\varepsilon}_i$ by  $\widehat{\< \cdot, \cdot \>}_i = 
R_i^{-2} \< \cdot, \cdot \>_i$, for $i =1,2$, and $\widehat{\< \cdot, \cdot \>}=\widehat{\< \cdot, \cdot \>}_1 + \widehat{\< \cdot, \cdot \>}_2$. 



Relative to the inner product $\widehat{\< \cdot, \cdot \>}$, $\overline{M}_i^2(\kappa_i)$  becomes $\overline{M}_i^2(\varepsilon)$, and so $f$ becomes an immersion $\hat f\colon M^3\to \overline{M}_1^2(\varepsilon)\times\overline{M}_2^2(\varepsilon)\subset (\mathbb{R}^{3, \varepsilon}_1 \times \mathbb{R}^{3, \varepsilon}_2, \widehat{\< \cdot, \cdot \>})$. Arguing exactly as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:scale}, one can prove the following proposition, which shows that $f$ is given as in~\ref{it:thm14}.



\begin{proposition} \label{prop:scale2}
  The metric induced by $\hat f$ on $M^3$ from $\widehat{\< \cdot, \cdot \>}$  has constant sectional curvature $\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$, and the shape operator of $\hat f$ also has rank $2$.
\end{proposition}



\begin{remark}
The preceding discussion applies to any hypersurface $f\colon M^3(\kappa)\to \overline{M}^2(\kappa_1)\times \overline{M}^2(\kappa_2)$ with $\operatorname{rk} S=2$ everywhere. However, we now show that, in particular, if its shape operator $S$ satisfies $S_{12}=0$, then $f$ is given as in Example \ref{ex:3.6}.

We observe that the condition $S_{12}=0$ is equivalent to requiring that $S\mathcal{R}= \mathcal{R} S$. 
Since any hypersurface $f\colon M^3(\kappa)\to \overline{M}^2(\kappa_1)\times \overline{M}^2(\kappa_2)$, with $\operatorname{rk} S=2$ everywhere, has a constant product angle function, it follows from \cite[Corollary~5.1]{CT2} that, under the assumption that $S\mathcal{R}= \mathcal{R} S$, it is given by \eqref{param}, with $f_1$ and $f_2$ as in \eqref{f1} and \eqref{f2}, respectively, for some $\theta\in \mathbb{R}$. The fact that $M^3$ has constant sectional curvature $\kappa=\frac{\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_+\kappa_2}$ now implies that
$\theta=\arcsin{\left(\frac{\kappa_1}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}\right)^{1/2}}$ and that the curvatures $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ of $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$, respectively, must be constants such that $\lambda_1\lambda_2=(\kappa_1\kappa_2)^{1/2}$, hence it is given as in Example \ref{ex:3.6}.
\end{remark}

\vspace{1ex}
To complete the proof of the theorem, it remains to prove that if a hypersurface $f\colon M^3(\kappa)\to \overline{M}^2(\kappa_1)\times \overline{M}^2(\kappa_2)$, with $\kappa_1, \kappa_2<0$, is as in \ref{it:thm13} in an open subset $\Omega\subset M^3(\kappa)$, then the same must hold on the entire $M^3(\kappa)$.

For a hypersurface $f\colon M^3(\kappa)\to \overline{M}^2(\kappa_1)\times \overline{M}^2(\kappa_2)$, $\kappa_1, \kappa_2<0$, as in~\ref{it:thm13}, the shape operator is given by $S=aI+b\mathcal{R}$, with $a$ and $b$ as in \eqref{eq:ab}. Therefore, the eigenvalues of $S$ are
$a=\frac{\kappa_1}{[-(\kappa_1+\kappa_2)]^{1/2}}$, $a+b=-\frac{\kappa_2}{[-(\kappa_1+\kappa_2)]^{1/2}}$, and $a+rb$, where $r\in(0,1)$ is an eigenvalue of $\mathcal{R}$. 
Suppose that the boundary $\partial \Omega$ of $ \Omega$ is nonempty. Then,
at a point $x\in M^3(\kappa)$ in $\partial \Omega$, there must exist a sequence $(x_n)$ in $\Omega$ converging to $x$ such that $a+r(x_n)b$ converges to $0$. Thus, $x$ also belongs to 
to the boundary $\partial \Omega'$ of the subset $\Omega'$ where $\operatorname{rk} S=2$ and $S\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{R} S$. On the other hand, at a point $(s, x_1, x_2)\in  \Omega'$, the nonzero principal curvatures are given by \eqref{eq:pc}. For $\theta=\arcsin \left(\frac{\kappa_1}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}\right)^{1/2}$, we have
$$\frac{\sin\theta}{R_1}= \frac{\kappa_1}{[-(\kappa_1+\kappa_2)]^{1/2}}, \quad \frac{\cos\theta}{R_2}= -\frac{\kappa_2}{[-(\kappa_1+\kappa_2)]^{1/2}},\quad \frac{\cos\theta}{R_1}= \left(- \frac{\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}\right)^{1/2}= \frac{\sin\theta}{R_2}$$
Thus, setting $K=\left(- \frac{\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}\right)^{1/2}$ and $d=\lambda_1R_1=\lambda_2R_2$, the nonzero principal curvatures can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\rho_1=-\frac{\kappa_1}{[-(\kappa_1+\kappa_2)]^{1/2}}\frac{-\sinh (Ks)+d\cosh(Ks)}{\cosh(Ks)-d\sinh(Ks)}
=\frac{\kappa_1}{[-(\kappa_1+\kappa_2)]^{1/2}}\frac{\tanh(Ks)-d}{1-d\tanh(Ks)}
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation*}
\rho_2=-\frac{\kappa_2}{[-(\kappa_1+\kappa_2)]^{1/2}}\frac{1-d\tanh(Ks)}{\tanh(Ks)-d}.
\end{equation*}
Therefore, for a sequence $(s_n, (x_1)_n, (x_2)_n)\in \Omega'$ converging to $x$, both sequences 
$\frac{\tanh(Ks_n)-d}{1-d\tanh(Ks_n)}$ and $\frac{1-d\tanh(Ks_n)}{\tanh(Ks_n)-d}$ must converge to $1$, which can only occur if 
$s_n\mapsto \infty$. This leads to a contradiction, establishing that no such point $x$ can exist. Consequently, we must have $\Omega=M^3(\kappa)$.

\smallskip
This completes the proof of the theorem.\hfill\qed

title: Proof
body_md:
For assertion~\ref{it:setcons1}, we first suppose that $n\ge 4$ and $\kappa\ne\tilde\kappa$. Let $j\colon\overline{M}^{n+2,\rho}(\tilde\kappa)\to \overline{M}^{n+3,\delta}(\kappa)$ be an umbilical isometric immersion, where  $\delta=\rho$ if $\tilde\kappa > \kappa$ and  $\delta=\rho+1$ if $\tilde\kappa < \kappa$. Let $F=j\circ \tilde f$. Then the second fundamental form $\mathrm{II}_{F}(x)$ of $F$ at any $x\in M^n$ is flat with respect to the inner product in the normal space $N_{F}M^n(x)$, which has index
 $$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} 0, \,\,\,\mbox{if either}\,\,\, \kappa_1, \kappa_2>0,\,\,\mbox{or}
 \,\,\, \kappa_1\kappa_2<0,\,\kappa_1+\kappa_2>0\,\,\,\mbox{and}\,\,\,\tilde\kappa > \kappa,\\
 2,  \,\,\,\mbox{if either}\,\,\,\kappa_1, \kappa_2<0\,\,\mbox{and}\,\, \tilde\kappa < \kappa,\,\,\mbox{or}
 \,\,\, \kappa_1\kappa_2<0,\, \kappa_1+\kappa_2<0\,\,\,\mbox{and} \,\,\tilde\kappa < \kappa,\\
 1, \,\,\,\mbox{in the remaining cases}.
 \end{array}\right.$$
  Notice that the inner product in the (one-dimensional) normal space to $j$ at $x$ is positive definite if $\tilde\kappa > \kappa$ and negative definite otherwise. Let $\nu$ be one of the two normal vectors to $j$ at $x$ such that $\<\nu, \nu\>=(\tilde\kappa - \kappa)/|\tilde\kappa - \kappa|$ and 
  $S_\nu= \sqrt{|\tilde\kappa - \kappa|}\,I$. In particular, the latter equation implies that $\mathrm{II}_F(x)$ has a trivial kernel.    
  
 The case in which the inner product on $N_F M^n(x)$ is positive definite is then ruled out by Lemma~\ref{lem:flatbi}\eqref{it:pode},
 which implies that $0=\dim \mathcal{N}(\mathrm{II}_{F}(x))\geq n-3$, in contradiction with the assumption that $n\geq 4$. 
 Multiplying by $-1$ the inner product on $N_FM^n(x)$ if it has index~$2$, it becomes a Lorentzian inner product. 
  Therefore, in the cases in which the inner product on $N_FM^n(x)$ has index either $1$ or $2$, Lemma~\ref{lem:flatbi}\eqref{it:symim} implies that the subspace $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_F(x))$ spanned by the image of $\mathrm{II}_F(x)$ must be degenerate for every $x\in M^n$, for otherwise we would reach the same contradiction as in the positive definite case. 

  Thus, there exists a nonzero vector $N\in \mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_F(x))\cap (\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_F(x)))^\perp$. Observe that $N$ cannot be orthogonal to $\nu$, as otherwise $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x))$ would be a degenerate subspace of a Lorentzian plane, and hence would be spanned by a light-like vector. This would imply that $\kappa =\tilde\kappa$ from Gauss equation of $\tilde f$, a contradiction. Consequently, we may assume that $N=i_*N_1+\nu$ for some $N_1 \in N_{\tilde{f}}M^n(x)$ with $\<N_1,N_1\> = \varepsilon = -(\tilde\kappa - \kappa)/|\tilde\kappa - \kappa|$. Since
    $$0=\<\mathrm{II}_{F}(X, Y), N\>=\<i_*\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(X, Y)+ \sqrt{|\tilde\kappa-\kappa|}\<X, Y\>\nu, i_*N_1+\nu\>,$$
    it follows that $S_{N_1} = \varepsilon\sqrt{|\tilde\kappa - \kappa|}I$.
    Choosing $N_2 \in N_{\tilde{f}}M^n(x)$ orthogonal to $N_1$ with $\<N_2,N_2\> = -\varepsilon$, Gauss equation of $\tilde{f}$ implies that $\operatorname{rk} S_{N_2} \le 1$. Therefore, $\{N_1,N_2\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $N_{\tilde{f}}M^n(x)$ such that
     $$S_{N_1}=\varepsilon \sqrt{|\tilde\kappa - \kappa|}\,I\,\,\,\mbox{and}\,\,\operatorname{rk} S_{N_2}\le 1.$$
    Now let $\theta \in C^\infty(M^n)$ be such that 
     $$i_*\xi=\cos \theta N_1+\sin \theta N_2 \,\,\,\,\mbox{and}\,\,\,\,V=-\sin\theta N_1+\cos\theta N_2.$$ 
     Then, on $\ker S_{N_2}$ we have
      $$S=\varepsilon\sqrt{|\tilde\kappa - \kappa|}\cos\theta\,I\,\,\, \mbox{and}\,\,\, aI+b\mathcal{R}=-\varepsilon\sqrt{|\tilde\kappa - \kappa|}\sin\theta\,I.$$
      Since $\dim\ker S_{N_2} \ge n-1$, it follows from the second of the above equations that $\mathcal{R}$ can have at most two distinct eigenvalues. As $\dim\ker\mathcal{R} \ge k-1 \ge 1$ and $\dim\ker(I-\mathcal{R})\ge n-k \ge 1$ by \eqref{dimkerR} and our assumption that $2\leq k\leq n-1$, such eigenvalues must be $0$ and $1$, with multiplicities  $(n-1, 1)$ or $(1, n-1)$. It follows from \eqref{dimkerR} that $k=n-1$ in the former case and $k=2$ in the latter. Moreover, $f$ is locally decomposable by Proposition~\ref{splits}; in particular, $\kappa=0$. But since both factors have dimensions greater than one and one of them is an inclusion,
     this leads to a contradiction.

     Now we have $\kappa=\tilde\kappa=\frac{\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}$. Then, at any $x\in M^n$, the second fundamental form $\mathrm{II}_{\tilde{f}}(x)$ is a flat bilinear form with respect to the inner product on $N_{\tilde{f}}M^n(x)$, whose index is equal to $\rho$. Therefore, if $\rho=0$, then $\dim\mathcal{N}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x)) \ge n-2$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:flatbi}\eqref{it:pode}.
     On the subspace $\mathcal{N}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f})$ at $x\in M^n$, we have $S=0=aI+b\mathcal{R}$. Since $-ab^{-1}=\kappa_1(\kappa_1+ \kappa_2)^{-1}$, by the assumption that $n\geq 4$ this contradicts the fact that the eigenvalues of $\mathcal{R}$ lie in $[0,1]$ and that the unique eigenvalue of $\mathcal{R}$ in $(0,1)$ has multiplicity one.
     Thus, we must have $\rho=1$, hence  $\kappa_1 \kappa_2<0$, with $\kappa_1+\kappa_2<0$, or $\kappa_1, \kappa_2<0$. 


     Next, when $n=\operatorname{rk} S=3$, the claim follows from \cite[Lemma~6(a)]{KNT}.

     We now prove assertion~\ref{it:setcons2}. Suppose that $n=3$ and $\operatorname{rk} S=2$. Arguing by contradiction, assume $\kappa\ne\tilde\kappa$. Then the same argument as in the case $n\ge 4$ applies, except that we must also consider the case in which the inner product on $N_{F}M^3(x)$ at a point $x\in M^3$ is positive definite. But then, since $\mathrm{II}_{F}(x)$ has trivial kernel, $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{F}(x))=N_{F}M^3(x)$. It follows from \cite[Theorem~5.2]{DT} that there exists a frame $\{X_1,X_2,X_3\}$ that diagonalises $\mathrm{II}_{F}$. As $S_{\nu}=\sqrt{|\tilde\kappa-\kappa|}I$, such a frame is orthogonal; hence, it may be chosen as an orthonormal frame. In particular, this frame diagonalises $\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}$ and so diagonalises $S$ and $aI+b\mathcal{R}$, thus $S\mathcal{R} = \mathcal{R} S$. We take $X_2=\|\zeta\|^{-1}\zeta$, then we obtain
     \begin{gather*}
         SX_1=\lambda_1 X_1,\quad SX_2=\lambda_2 X_2,\quad SX_3=\lambda_3 X_3,\\
         \mathcal{R} X_1 = 0,\quad \mathcal{R} X_2 = r X_2, \quad \mathcal{R} X_3 = X_3,\\
         (I-\mathcal{R})X_1 = X_1,\quad (I-\mathcal{R})X_2 = (1-r)X_2,\quad (I-\mathcal{R})X_3 = 0.
     \end{gather*}
     Gauss equation~\eqref{Gauss} gives $\kappa=\lambda_1\lambda_2 + \kappa_1(1-r)  = \lambda_2\lambda_3+\kappa_2 r = \lambda_1\lambda_3$. This yields $\lambda_1\lambda_3\ne 0$ and so $\lambda_2=0$ as $\operatorname{rk} S =2$. Moreover, we have $\kappa_1(1-r)=\kappa=\kappa_2 r$, which implies $\kappa=\frac{\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}=\tilde\kappa$, a contradiction. 
     
     Now we have $\kappa=\frac{\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}$. Then, $\mathrm{II}_{\tilde{f}}(x)$ is a flat bilinear form for every $x\in M^3$, and hence it has nontrivial kernel by Lemma~\ref{lem:flatbi}\eqref{it:pode}. In particular, $S_{V} = aI + b\mathcal{R}$ has nontrivial kernel and $r=-ab^{-1} = \kappa_1(\kappa_1+\kappa_2)^{-1}$. Since $\mathcal{N}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}) = \ker S \cap \ker S_V$, a vector field $Y$ spanning $\mathcal{N}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f})$ satisfies $SY= 0 $ and $\mathcal{R} Y = rY$. Computing the sectional curvatures of the planes spanned by $\{X,Y\}$ and $\{Y,Z\}$, where $\{X,Y,Z\}$ is an orthonormal frame such that $\mathcal{R} X = 0$ and $\mathcal{R} Z= Z$, and using Gauss equation of $F$, we have $\kappa_1(1-r)=\kappa=\kappa_2 r$, which implies $\kappa_1\kappa_2>0$.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: flatH} 
If $f\colon M^n\to \mathbb{R}^k\times \mathbb{H}^{n-k+1}\subset \mathbb{R}^k\times \mathbb{R}^{n-k+2, 1}=\mathbb{R}^{n+2, 1}
$,
$
1\leq k\leq n-3,
$ 
is a flat hypersurface, then $f(M^n)$ is an open subset of the intersection of $\mathbb{R}^k\times \mathbb{H}^{n-k+1}$ with an affine hyperplane $\mathcal{H}$  of $\mathbb{R}^{n+2, 1}$ orthogonal to a light-like vector $w\in \mathbb{R}^{n+2, 1}$. Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}[label={\rm{(\roman*)}}]
\item\label{it:flat1} if $w\in \mathbb{R}^{n-k+2, 1}$, then $f(M^n)$ is an open subset of the image of an extrinsic product
$$
\operatorname{id}\times g\colon \mathbb{R}^{k}\times \mathbb{R}^{n-k}\to \mathbb{R}^{k}\times \mathbb{H}^{n-k+1},
$$
where 
$
g\colon  \mathbb{R}^{n-k}\to  \mathbb{H}^{n-k+1}
$ 
is a horosphere and  
$
\operatorname{id} \colon \mathbb{R}^{k}\to \mathbb{R}^{k}
$ 
is the identity map;

\smallskip
\item\label{it:flat2} if $w\not\in \mathbb{R}^{n-k+2, 1}$, then $f(M^n)$ is an open subset of the image of an extrinsic product
$$
\operatorname{id}\times g\colon \mathbb{R}^{k-1}\times \mathbb{R}^{n-k+1}\to \mathbb{R}^{k-1}\times(\mathbb{R}\times  \mathbb{H}^{n-k+1}),
$$
where 
$
g\colon  \mathbb{R}^{n-k+1}\to \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{H}^{n-k+1}
$ 
is an isometric immersion, whose image is a {\rm(}complete flat{\rm)} spherical rotational hypersurface
by  \cite[Theorem~7.2$({\rm iii})-({\rm c})$]{MaT}, and 
$
\operatorname{id} \colon \mathbb{R}^{k-1}\to \mathbb{R}^{k-1}
$ 
is the identity map.
\end{enumerate}

label: ineq
title: Proof
body_md:
Let 
$
j \colon \mathbb{R}^k\times \mathbb{H}^{n-k+1}\to \mathbb{R}^k\times\mathbb{R}^{n-k+2,1}=\mathbb{R}^{n+2,1}
$ 
be the inclusion,  and let 
$
\tilde f=j \circ f \colon  M^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n+2,1} 
$ 
be its composition with $f$. 
Flatness of $M^n$ implies that $\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x)$
is a flat bilinear form for any $x \in M^n$, with respect to the Lorentzian inner product in $N_{\tilde f}M^n(x)$. If $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x))$ was nondegenerate, that is, $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x)) \cap \mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x))^{\perp} = \{0\}$, then
$
\dim  \mathcal{N}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x)) \geq n-2
$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:flatbi}\eqref{it:symim}, 
and since $\mathcal{N}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x))=\ker S(x)\cap \ker \mathcal{R}(x)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{ineq}
n-2\leq \dim (\ker S(x)\cap \ker \mathcal{R}(x))\leq \dim  \ker \mathcal{R}(x) \leq k,
\end{equation} 
a contradiction. Thus, $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(x))$ is degenerate for every $x\in M^n$. Then, for a choice of one of the two unit normal vectors $\xi$ to $f$ in $\mathbb{R}^k \times \mathbb{H}^{n-k+1}$,  the subspace $\mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f})\cap \mathcal{I}(\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f})^{\perp}$ is spanned by the light-like vector $\nu=j_*\xi - \nu_2$, where $\nu_2=\tilde{\pi}_2\circ \tilde{f}$, with $\tilde{\pi}_2\colon \mathbb{R}^{n+2,1}\to  \mathbb{R}^{n-k+2,1}$ the orthogonal projection.  Using the first equation in \eqref{eq:nu'}, this implies that 
\begin{equation*}
    0 = \< \mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(X,Y),  j_*\xi - \nu_2 \> = \<   \<SX,Y\> j_*\xi - \<\mathcal{R} X,Y\>\nu_2, j_*\xi - \nu_2 \> = \<SX,Y\> - \<\mathcal{R} X,Y\> 
\end{equation*}
 for all $X,Y \in \Gamma(TM^n)$, hence $S=\mathcal{R}$.  Therefore,
 $
\mathrm{II}_{\tilde f}(X,Y)=\<\mathcal{R} X,Y\>\nu
$
  for all $X,Y \in \Gamma(TM^n)$. Now, using the second equation in \eqref{eq:nu'}, we have
  $$
\nabla_X^\perp \nu =
\nabla_X^\perp j_*\xi-
\nabla_X^\perp \nu_2\\
=\<X, \zeta\>(-j_*\xi+f_2)\\
= -\<X, \zeta\>\nu.
 $$
Notice that by Lemma~\ref{lem:grad} the vector field  $\zeta$ is a gradient vector field. Taking (locally) a positive $\lambda\in C^{\infty}(M^n)$ such that 
$\mbox{grad\,}(\log\lambda)= \zeta$ implies that $w=\lambda\nu$ is a constant vector in $\mathbb{R}^{n+2,1}$, for $S^{\tilde f}_w=0$ and 
 $$\nabla_X^\perp w=X(\lambda)\nu+\lambda \nabla_X^\perp \nu=\<\mbox{grad\,} \lambda, X\>\nu-\lambda\<X,\zeta\>\nu=0.$$ Therefore,  $\tilde f(M^n)$ is contained in the intersection of $\mathbb{R}^k\times \mathbb{H}^{n-k+1}\subset \mathbb{R}^{n+2,1}$ with an affine (degenerate) hyperplane $\mathcal{H}$ orthogonal to $w$.

 If $w\in \mathbb{R}^{n-k+2, 1}$, then $\tilde{f}(M^n)\subset \mathbb{R}^k\times (\mathbb{H}^{n-k+1}\cap \mathcal{H})$, and \ref{it:flat1} holds. Otherwise,
 $w\in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}^{n-k+2, 1}$, up to an orthogonal transformation of $\mathbb{R}^{n+2, 1}$, hence
 \[\tilde{f}(M^n)\subset \mathbb{R}^{k-1}\times ((\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{H}^{n-k+1})\cap \mathcal{H}),\] and \ref{it:flat2} holds for the 
 flat hypersurface $(\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{H}^{n-k+1})\cap \mathcal{H}\subset \mathbb{R}^{n-k+2, 1}$ of $\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{H}^{n-k+1}$.

The case in which $k=1$ and $n=3$ is not covered under the assumption $1\leq k\leq n-3$ of Theorem \ref{thm: flatH}. Following the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: flatH}, we see that the inequalities \eqref{ineq} do not lead to a contradiction in this case, but rather imply that
 $\dim \ker \mathcal{R}(x)=1=k$ for every $x\in M^3$.
 Then, Proposition~\ref{splits} implies that $f$ is locally decomposable, and, since $M^3$ is flat, $f$ is a vertical cylinder over a flat surface in $\mathbb{H}^3$.
 This corresponds to  \cite[Theorem~7.2(iii)-(a)]{MaT} in the classification of hypersurfaces with constant sectional curvature of $\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{H}^n$.
